t.segment cajay huaritambo@-9.3,-77.1:
Few riders ever get this far into the Conchucos, the deep valleys on the eastern side of Peru's Cordillera Blanca, and that is half the reason to come. The label refers to a stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network that ran for thousands of kilometres along the Andes, here crossing between the hamlet of Cajay and Huaritambo, whose name preserves the word tambo, the waystation where runners and travellers on imperial business could rest, eat and change loads. Parts of the paving, retaining walls and drainage channels still survive on slopes where it is hard to imagine anyone building anything at all.

Getting here is the adventure. The nearest place of any size listed is Yauya, more than thirty kilometres away by road that will feel much longer, and between them lie switchbacks of dirt and rock carved into mountainsides, river crossings after rain, and the occasional landslide that closes a road for a day. Altitude is the real opponent: the passes in this part of Ancash climb well above four thousand metres, and both rider and engine will feel it. Go slowly, drink a lot, and do not plan a schedule tighter than the mountains allow. The dry season, roughly May to September, gives firm surfaces and clear mornings; the wet months bring mud and clouds that sit on the road.

The landscape changes with every hundred metres of height. Down in the valleys there are eucalyptus, maize terraces and small adobe villages; higher up the grass thins into puna, where the wind is cold even in sun and the only company might be a farmer with sheep or a few llamas. The Inca engineers chose lines that work for walkers and pack animals, not for vehicles, so the modern track and the ancient road cross and diverge; where they meet, it is worth stopping, cutting the engine and walking a few hundred metres of the old stones. You get a sense of how an empire held together a country this vertical.

Practical matters need real planning. Fuel in this region is often sold from drums in villages, and quality varies, so fill up properly in the larger towns and carry a reserve. Yauya and the other district capitals have small shops, simple restaurants serving soup, potatoes, trout or cuy, and basic lodging. Phone signal comes and goes. Carry cash in small notes, warm layers and a basic repair kit; the people are generous, but the nearest workshop may be a day away.
t.huascaran national park@-9.3,-77.4:
The Cordillera Blanca is the highest tropical mountain range on earth, and Huascarán National Park protects most of it: dozens of peaks over six thousand metres, hundreds of glaciers and glacial lakes, and high valleys of grass and rock. Huascarán itself, at 6,768 metres, is the highest mountain in Peru, a twin-summited giant of ice and snow that dominates the Callejón de Huaylas, the long valley of the Santa river below. The park was listed by UNESCO in 1985, and it is one of the great mountain landscapes of the world.

The mountains have a terrible side. In 1970, an earthquake triggered an avalanche of ice and rock from Huascarán that buried the town of Yungay, killing thousands of people in minutes. The site of the old town is now a memorial park, with the tops of palm trees from the main square still visible above the debris. Nearby, the Llanganuco lakes, two turquoise lagoons in a deep valley beneath Huascarán, are among the most beautiful places in the park.

Riding here is an unforgettable experience, but a demanding one. The road from Huaraz north through the Callejón de Huaylas is paved and busy, with views of the snowy peaks on one side and the Cordillera Negra on the other. The roads into the park climb to extreme altitudes: the road from Carhuaz through the Punta Olímpica tunnel to Chacas, on the eastern side, climbs well above four thousand metres in a series of hairpins with glaciers right above you, and the road to the Llanganuco lakes continues over a high pass on a dirt surface. Altitude sickness is a real risk, so acclimatise in Huaraz for a few days before going higher. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time to visit.

Huaraz, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the main base, with fuel, shops, hotels, restaurants and mountain guides. Carhuaz is a smaller town with fuel and a famous ice cream shop. Local food includes trout, potatoes in endless varieties and pachamanca, meat and vegetables cooked underground on hot stones. There is a park entrance fee for some areas. Carry warm clothing, sun protection and plenty of water, as conditions change rapidly in the mountains.
t.segment ayash taulli@-9.5,-77.0:
East of the Cordillera Blanca, the Andes break into a jumble of high plateaus and deep valleys draining toward the Marañón and the Amazon, and the Inca road ran through this country on its way from Cusco to Quito. The Ayash to Taulli segment is a stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan in the highlands of Huánuco, near the town of Llata, part of the UNESCO-listed Andean road system. It runs through the puna, the high grassland above the tree line, where the wind blows cold and the views stretch for miles over ridges and valleys. In places, the original road survives, with stone paving, retaining walls, steps and drainage channels, and walking a section of it is the best way to understand how the Incas moved people and goods across this vertical landscape.

Not far to the south lies Huánuco Pampa, one of the most important Inca administrative centres, a huge plaza with a ceremonial platform, storehouses and palaces on a high plain near La Unión. It was a stop on the main road, and its ruins are among the most impressive in the central Andes, though few tourists make it there.

Riding in this region is for the adventurous. Roads are mostly unpaved, with steep climbs, hairpins, landslides and river crossings, and altitudes regularly exceed four thousand metres. Distances are long and services few, so careful planning is essential. The rainy season, from November to April, can make roads impassable, so the dry season is the time to come. Weather can change quickly, with sun, hail and snow in the same day, and nights are freezing.

Llata, about twenty-seven kilometres away, is a small provincial capital with basic services, and fuel may be available, though perhaps not always of the highest quality. La Unión, near Huánuco Pampa, is another option, and Huánuco city, much further east and lower down, has full services. Carry extra fuel, food, water, warm clothing and repair tools, and be prepared to rely on the hospitality of local people, who are generally friendly and helpful. The local food is simple but nourishing: soups, potatoes, cheese and roasted guinea pig.
t.segment taparaku tambo de llata@-9.6,-76:
The Qhapaq Ñan, the great road network of the Inca Empire, ran for thousands of kilometres along the Andes, linking the capital Cusco with the far corners of an empire that stretched from Colombia to Chile. In the department of Huánuco, in central Peru, one of its best preserved sections crosses the high puna between the administrative centre of Huánuco Pampa and the valleys to the north, and the segment between Taparaku and the Tambo de Llata is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2014.

The road was built with remarkable engineering: stone paving, retaining walls, drainage channels and stairways that carried it over mountains and across valleys. Along the way, tambos, rest houses and storage centres, provided food and shelter for officials, soldiers and messengers, the chasquis who ran in relays to carry messages across the empire. Huánuco Pampa, near the town of La Unión, was one of the largest Inca administrative centres, with a huge central plaza and an ushnu, a ceremonial platform.

Riding in this part of the Andes is an adventure. The roads are often unpaved, rough and dusty in the dry season and muddy in the rainy season, from December to March. Altitudes are high, often over 3,500 metres, which affects both riders and engines. The landscape is vast and empty, with grasslands, lakes and snow-capped peaks, and villages are few and far between. Distances that look short on a map can take hours. Plan carefully, carry spare fuel, water and food, and be prepared for sudden changes in weather, including cold nights and afternoon storms.

La Unión and Llata, both about thirty kilometres away, are small towns with basic services, though fuel may be limited and of variable quality. Local people are generally friendly and helpful, and speaking some Spanish helps. Food in the highlands is simple but nourishing: soups, potatoes in countless varieties and cuy, roasted guinea pig, a traditional Andean dish. Walking a section of the Inca road, with the paving stones still in place after five centuries, is a powerful experience.
t.segment cotocancha alturas de torre@-8.7:
High on the eastern side of the Cordillera Blanca, in the Conchucos valleys of Ancash, a stretch of the old Inca road crosses grassy ridges between Cotocancha and the heights known as Alturas de Torre. This is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the vast Andean road network that tied the Inca empire together, inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014. The main trunk here ran north from Huánuco Pampa towards Cajamarca, and in places you can still see stone paving, retaining walls, drainage channels and steps.

The road was built for walkers, llama caravans and runners carrying messages, not for wheels, so it climbs and drops more steeply than any modern road would. Following it on foot for even a short distance gives you a sense of the Inca genius for engineering, with routes chosen to stay on firm ground and stone laid to resist torrential rains.

The nearest town is Pomabamba, about nine kilometres away, a small provincial capital at around 3,000 metres known for its hot springs and its festivals, and a base for treks into the Cordillera Blanca. The landscape is dramatic: deep valleys, cultivated slopes with fields of potatoes and maize, eucalyptus groves near villages and grassland above, with glaciated peaks visible on clear days.

Riding in the Conchucos is serious adventure riding. Roads are often unpaved or partly paved, narrow, with steep drops, landslides in the rainy season from about December to March, and long stretches without services. Altitude matters: you will be riding well above 3,000 metres, sometimes over 4,000, which affects both rider and engine. Acclimatise, drink plenty of water and carry warm layers, as temperatures drop sharply after sunset. The dry season, from May to September, offers the best conditions and the clearest views.

Fuel in Pomabamba and other small towns may be sold from drums or small stations, and quality varies. Carry a spare and fill whenever you can. People in the region speak Quechua as well as Spanish, and a few words of greeting go a long way. Food is simple and filling: soups, potatoes, trout from mountain streams and, at festivals, pachamanca, meat and potatoes cooked in an earth oven.
t.segment tambo chico taparaku@-9.7,-76.8:
The Qhapaq Ñan, the royal road of the Incas, linked an empire that stretched from what is now Colombia to Chile and Argentina, and in the highlands of Huánuco in central Peru one of its best-preserved stretches runs across the high puna between Tambo Chico and Taparaku. The coordinates put it in the high country north of La Unión, at an altitude where the air is thin, the grass is golden and the sky seems close enough to touch.

This section of the Inca road is part of the main highland route that ran from Cusco north to Quito, and it is famous for the quality of its construction: stone paving, retaining walls, drainage channels, steps on steep slopes and stone causeways across marshy ground. Every so often along the road stood tambos, way stations where runners, soldiers and officials could rest and find supplies. Not far away, near La Unión, lies Huánuco Pampa, also called Huánuco Viejo, one of the largest Inca administrative centres, with a vast plaza and a ceremonial platform. The road network was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014 as a transnational site shared by six countries.

Riding here is a high-altitude adventure. The roads into this area are mostly unpaved, with gravel, dust, mud after rain and some steep, rocky sections, and they climb to well over three thousand five hundred metres. Altitude affects riders and bikes alike: take time to acclimatise in the lower valleys, drink plenty of water and be alert to headaches and breathlessness. Engines lose power and fuel injection may struggle. The wet season, roughly from December to March, makes the tracks slippery and can cut off roads entirely; the dry winter months, from May to September, bring clear skies, cold nights and the best conditions.

Fuel is scarce. La Unión, about twenty kilometres away, and Llata are small towns with limited facilities, and fuel there may come from small stations or drums; fill up wherever you can and carry a reserve. Bring warm clothes, rain gear and some food, as there is little along the way.

The people of these highlands are mostly Quechua-speaking farmers and herders, and you will pass llamas, sheep and potato fields on the slopes. Greet them, ask before taking photographs, and enjoy a bowl of hot soup in a village eatery. Walking even a short way along the Inca road, on stones laid more than five hundred years ago, is a quiet thrill.
t.church of the intercession on the river:
A small white church stands alone in a meadow where two rivers meet, and on still days it is mirrored in the water. The Church of the Intercession on the Nerl was built in 1165 by Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky of Vladimir-Suzdal, and it has become something close to a national symbol in Russia: a perfect, slender building of white limestone, with a single dome and carved reliefs of King David, lions and griffins on its walls. It is part of the White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal, listed by UNESCO in 1992.

The church was built on an artificial mound at the confluence of the Nerl and the Klyazma, designed to withstand the spring floods that turn the meadows into a lake. Even now, in spring, the church can sometimes be reached only by boat. The rest of the year, it is a walk of a little over a kilometre from the village of Bogolyubovo along a path through the meadows, and the approach, with the church slowly growing larger on the horizon, is part of the experience.

Bogolyubovo itself was Andrei's residence, and parts of his palace survive within the walls of a later monastery. Andrei was a powerful and ruthless prince who sacked Kiev and moved the centre of power north-east; he was murdered by his own boyars in 1174 in this very palace. A few kilometres away, Vladimir, his capital, preserves the Golden Gate and the cathedrals of the Assumption and of Saint Demetrius, the latter covered in extraordinary stone carvings.

For riders, the main approach is along the M7 highway from Moscow, a busy road with heavy truck traffic, so it is better to use smaller roads where possible. The countryside of the Vladimir region is gentle and rolling, with birch forests, fields and small villages of wooden houses, and the quieter roads toward Suzdal, a small town full of churches and monasteries, are a pleasure to ride. Note that at present, travel to Russia is restricted for many nationalities, and anyone considering a trip should check current official advice first.

Vladimir, around twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind. In Suzdal, look out for medovukha, a traditional honey drink, and for pickled cucumbers, a local speciality celebrated with a festival in summer. The best times to visit are early summer, when the meadows are green, and autumn, when the birches turn gold.
t.segment tambillo pincosh@-9.4,-77.1:
This is high, remote country. The Tambillo to Pincosh segment of the Qhapaq Ñan crosses the puna of the Ancash and Huánuco highlands, east of the Cordillera Blanca, at altitudes of around four thousand metres, part of the stretch of the Inca road that ran north from Cusco through the Andes towards Quito. The road here was the main artery of the empire, with tambos, way stations, every day's walk or so, where travellers, messengers and armies could rest and find supplies. Tambillo, the little tambo, suggests one of those stations. Today, the road survives as a stone-paved path with retaining walls and drainage channels, crossing open grassland, wetlands and passes, and it is one of the best-preserved sections of the network, listed by UNESCO along with the rest of the Qhapaq Ñan.

The Cordillera Blanca, to the west, is the highest tropical mountain range in the world, with dozens of peaks over six thousand metres, including Huascarán, the highest mountain in Peru. The Huascarán National Park, a UNESCO site, protects glaciers, lakes, and the strange Puya raimondii, a giant bromeliad that can grow over ten metres tall and flowers only once in its long life before dying. On the eastern side of the range, the land drops towards the Amazon basin through deep valleys, and the communities live from herding, potatoes and grains.

The riding is for experienced adventurers only. The roads in this region are mostly unpaved, with steep climbs, hairpins, mud, rocks and river crossings, and they can be blocked by landslides in the rainy season, from December to March. Distances are long, and services are few. Altitude is a serious factor: acclimatise in Huaraz for several days, and watch for signs of altitude sickness. The weather changes quickly, with snow possible at any time of year on the passes, and the nights are freezing.

The nearest town with services is Llata, about thirty kilometres away, a small provincial capital, and fuel may be limited. Carry extra fuel, water, food, warm clothing and tools, and let someone know your route. Ask locally about road conditions before setting out. The rewards are immense: empty landscapes, glaciers, lakes, and the sense of following in the footsteps of Inca messengers.
t.the historic town and archaeological sit:
Gedi does not announce itself. You drive along the Kenyan coast through palms, cashew trees and roadside stalls selling mangoes, turn in under the shade of the Arabuko-Sokoke forest, and suddenly there are coral-stone walls in the trees, a mosque with an arched doorway, a palace courtyard, houses with wells and sleeping niches, all roofed with branches and leaves instead of stone. This was a Swahili town, founded around the twelfth century and flourishing in the fifteenth, when it traded with the Indian Ocean world, with Chinese porcelain and Venetian glass turning up in the digging. By the early seventeenth century the people had gone. Nobody knows exactly why, and the theories, a shift of the coast, raids, or the failure of the water, have never been settled.

The forest swallowed it, and the effect today is of a ruined city under a green roof. Vervet and Sykes monkeys leap along the walls, hornbills call, butterflies drift along the paths, and a guide will point out the big baobab and the ceremonial gate, as well as the toilets, which were remarkably advanced. The silence between the stones is the real attraction, and an early morning visit, before the heat and the tour vans, is best.

The ride from Mombasa is a long day, roughly a hundred kilometres north along the coast road through Mtwapa and Kilifi, with a mix of fast, flat road, villages, speed bumps and trucks. Traffic can be chaotic around towns, and drivers overtake with optimism, so keep a wide margin. The surface is mostly good, but potholes appear after rains. Malindi, a town of more than a hundred thousand, is a few kilometres further and has plenty of fuel, restaurants and hotels, and a long beach.

Heat and humidity are heavy, so go early and drink water. The dry seasons, from January to March and from July to October, are the best times, as the long rains from April to June can turn the red earth tracks to mud. Eat fresh grilled fish, coconut rice or sweet mahamri bread for breakfast, and bring a hat and insect repellent for the forest walk, because mosquitoes and ticks do not respect history.
t.segment lomas de huarin matacocha@-8.8,-:
Few places in Peru feel as far from Lima as the eastern side of the Cordillera Blanca, in the Conchucos country of the Ancash region. The Inca road here was a mountain track, climbing from the valley of the Marañón up to the high grasslands, and the segment from Lomas de Huarin to Matacocha, part of the UNESCO Qhapaq Ñan listing of 2014, runs through a landscape of steep green slopes, terraced fields, small hamlets and a sky that feels very close. The towns are Pomabamba, a market town known for hot springs, and Yauya, a smaller place in a side valley, with farms and a busy Sunday market.

The Conchucos people were fierce enough that the Incas needed years to subdue them, and they left behind stone towers, burial houses and fortified hilltop settlements. Today the valleys are farmland, with potatoes, maize and wheat in small plots, and mule trains still carry loads along the older tracks. Quechua is spoken in the villages, and visitors are greeted warmly if they arrive with patience.

I cannot say precisely where the segment lies, so treat the label as a pointer to the region. The riding, however, is clear. The road from Huaraz crosses the Cordillera Blanca by the Punta Olímpica pass, at around four thousand seven hundred metres, one of the highest paved passes in the Americas, with a tunnel at the crest and views of glaciers and peaks over six thousand metres. Beyond it the road descends to Chacas and further to the Conchucos valleys, with hairpins, rough patches and cattle. Fuel is easy in Huaraz, but scarce in small towns, so carry spare and top up whenever you can. Weather changes fast, and cold, hail and fog can arrive in an hour.

The dry months from May to September give the clearest views, though nights are freezing. The rainy season turns tracks into mud and brings landslides. Altitude is a serious factor, so spend a couple of days in Huaraz before the pass, and carry warm clothes, snacks and water. After a long day, the hot pools at Pomabamba are the best reward a rider can imagine.
t.segment huanuco pampa huaricashash@-9.9,:
Huanuco Pampa is a place that makes you feel small. On a high plateau at around 3,700 metres, in the central Peruvian Andes, the Incas built one of their largest administrative centres, on the great highway that ran north from Cusco toward Quito. Archaeologists have counted hundreds of storehouses on the surrounding hillsides, once filled with maize, textiles and weapons, and the ruins of a huge central plaza, with a platform called the usnu from which the Inca or his representative could watch ceremonies. It is part of the Qhapaq Nan, the Andean road system recognised by UNESCO in 2014.

The road itself is the real story. The Incas had no wheels and no horses, but they built some forty thousand kilometres of paved and stepped paths across mountains and deserts, with rest houses and relay runners, so that news could travel hundreds of kilometres a day. The segment that links Huanuco Pampa to Huaricashash is a stretch of that network, with its stone paving and retaining walls still in place on the high grassland. Walking even a short section gives a sense of how carefully it was engineered.

Getting there on a motorbike is an expedition rather than a day ride. The roads that climb to the plateau from the Huallaga and Maranon valleys are rough, narrow and sometimes unpaved, with steep drops, loose stone, and landslides in the rainy season, which runs roughly from December to March. At this altitude, engines lose power and riders lose breath, and the weather swings from fierce sun to hail within an hour. The dry months, from May to September, are the only sensible time to go, and nights can be bitterly cold.

La Unión is the nearest settlement, a small town with basic shops and a few places to eat, while larger towns, such as San Miguel de Cauri, are farther away, and Huanuco city lies a long way down the valleys. Fuel is scarce and sometimes sold from drums, so carry a spare can, plenty of water, and warm clothes. The people here speak Quechua as well as Spanish, and a few words of greeting are warmly received.
t.segment quinrraycueva pariachuco@-8.4,-7:
The Inca built roads the way other empires built walls, as a statement of power, and the high stretches in the northern Andes of Peru show it best. This segment of the Qhapaq Nan, the great network that the Incas extended over some thirty thousand kilometres, runs through steep country between the Santa river canyon and the high valleys of Conchucos, where the road goes where it must, up flights of stone steps, along retaining walls and across ravines on bridges of woven grass rope. I cannot name a village for this stretch, and the label gives only a pair of old place names, but the character is clear.

The Incas had no wheeled vehicles and no horses. The roads were for feet and llamas, and for the chasquis, the relay runners who carried messages and goods from one waystation, or tambo, to the next, so that a message could cover hundreds of kilometres in days. Along the road were storehouses, rest houses and administrative centres, all feeding the machinery of the state. In 2014, UNESCO listed the network in six countries, Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, as the Qhapaq Nan Andean Road System.

For the rider, the paved roads in this part of Peru are remarkable in themselves. From the coast, road climbs from the desert to the cordillera in a series of hairpins and tunnels, reaching puna grassland above four thousand metres, with cold air, thin oxygen and long views of snow peaks. Fuel is available in larger towns, but distances between them can be great, and a lot of the secondary roads are gravel and rock. Landslides, falling stones and animals on the road are regular hazards. Do not ride at night.

If you have not travelled at altitude before, give yourself days to adjust, drink water, and keep a slow pace. Coca tea, which you will be offered everywhere, helps with the symptoms.

The dry season, from May to September, is the time to go, with sunny days and freezing nights. Between December and March the rain brings mud and slides. The best way to appreciate the road is to leave the bike and walk a section, feeling the worn stone under your boots.
t.segment pariachuco tauli@-8.3,-77.8:
Some roads you can still feel. At this part of the northern Peruvian Andes, the old Inca road survives as a worn stone staircase and a retaining wall, the surface polished by centuries of llamas and sandals, with drainage channels still carrying water off the path. It belongs to the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road system that was listed by UNESCO in 2014, and this segment, which the label ties to two places called Pariachuco and Tauli, shows what the engineering was like at its best. Where a slope was steep, the builders cut steps; where a cliff was in the way, they cut a ledge; where a stream crossed, they set stepping stones or built a bridge of stone slabs.

I do not know these two places by name, so let me describe what surrounds them. The coordinates lie in the northern highlands of Ancash, high above the Pacific coast, in a country of terraced hillsides, small adobe villages and slopes that go from desert-dry to cloud-forest green with changes in altitude. Quechua is still spoken here, and people in bright skirts and felt hats herd sheep and cattle along the old tracks. Potatoes, maize, quinoa and many local crops grow in small fields on steep slopes, often sown by hand, as they have been for millennia.

Riding here demands care. Mountain roads in Peru are narrow, often unpaved, and the edge is frequently a long way down, with trucks and buses that assume the middle of the road is theirs. Rock falls, wandering livestock and sudden weather are everyday risks. Fuel is found in towns, not villages, so plan and carry spare. Altitude can be a challenge for both rider and engine, as carburetted bikes lose power and fuel-injected ones cope better.

Thick afternoon cloud often rolls in during the wet season, which runs from December to March, so start early. The dry season, from May to October, brings brilliant light and cold nights.

Respect the people, ask before photographing, and buy something from the village shop, because that is how places like this survive. A cup of hot soup, caldo de gallina, is a welcome treat after a cold ride.
t.the golden@56.1,40.4:
Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky built a gate to impress, and eight and a half centuries later it still does. The Golden Gate of Vladimir was raised in 1164 as the ceremonial entrance to the capital of the principality, a white limestone arch with massive oak doors covered in gilded copper, topped by a small church, and designed to show visitors coming from the west that this was the rising power of Russia. Andrei, who moved his capital here from Kiev's orbit, founded a whole new centre of Russian culture on the bluffs above the Klyazma river, and the white stone cathedrals he and his brother built were models for Russian church architecture.

The gate survived the sack of Vladimir by the Mongols in 1238, when the city was burned and its people massacred, though it was damaged, and later centuries made repairs and additions. Today it houses a small museum of the city's military history, which you can climb to for a view of the town. A short walk away stands the Dormition Cathedral, begun in 1158, with its golden dome and the frescoes by Andrei Rublev and Daniil Chorny from the early fifteenth century. Some twelve kilometres east, in the flood meadows of the Nerl river, is the tiny, perfect Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, which many call the most beautiful church in Russia.

Vladimir sits on the Golden Ring, the circuit of historic towns north-east of Moscow, and Suzdal, with its monasteries, wooden churches and pickle fairs, is about thirty-five kilometres away. The city is about two hundred kilometres east of Moscow along the M7 highway, a busy road with heavy truck traffic and frequent speed cameras. Vladimir itself, with over three hundred thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and hotels.

The countryside is rolling, wooded and cut by rivers, with villages of wooden houses with painted shutters. Summer is warm and green, and autumn brings gold and mist. Winters are cold, with snow, and the churches look best against a white sky.

Locals will tell you about Vladimir cherries, an old local variety, and about gingerbread. Check current travel conditions before planning any trip into Russia, since foreign visitors face significant restrictions.
t.old city of sana a@15.4,44.2:
Sana'a is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and its old quarter, a tight maze of tall mud-brick and stone houses, looks almost impossibly intricate. The buildings rise six or seven storeys, their facades decorated with white gypsum patterns around the windows, and the windows themselves are often filled with coloured glass that glows in the evening. The city lies on a high plateau, at about 2,200 metres in the mountains of Yemen, and the air is thin and dry and bright.

Legend gives the founding to Shem, the son of Noah, and the city certainly existed long before Islam arrived. It was an important stop on the incense and spice routes, and under Islam it became a major centre of learning, with dozens of mosques. The Great Mosque is one of the earliest in the world. Inside the old walls are markets, called souks, grouped by trade, selling spices, silverware, coffee and daggers. The city's character comes from the ways in which these buildings were adapted to a crowded, high-altitude world, with rooftop gardens and tall towers called tower houses.

For visitors, the biggest issue is safety. Yemen has been in a state of conflict since 2014, and travel advice from most governments warns against going, so this is a place to read about, and visit only when the situation allows. The old city is on UNESCO's list of sites in danger, damaged by airstrikes and neglect.

If travel were feasible, the road to Ma'rib across the desert plateau would take you to the ruins of an ancient dam, said to be linked to the legendary kingdom of Sheba, and the mountain roads are spectacular. The capital has fuel and food, and in peacetime the cafes serve strong coffee flavoured with ginger and honey, along with flatbread, lamb and a stew called saltah. Please check official guidance carefully and never plan a ride here on the basis of old information.
t.khoy@38.5,44.6:
Khoy is the big, practical city of Iran's far north-west, a place of about a hundred and seventy-five thousand people on a wide fertile plain between the Turkish border and Lake Urmia. It is not a showpiece. It is a working town of bazaars, apricot and grape growers, trucking depots and solid apartment blocks, and that is exactly what makes it useful. This is where you buy supplies, change money, find a proper meal and get fuel before the road climbs toward the mountains.

The history is older than the concrete suggests. Khoy lay on the trade route between Tabriz and Anatolia, and caravans have been passing through for centuries. The town claims a link to Shams-e Tabrizi, the wandering mystic who became the teacher of the poet Rumi, and a tomb associated with him draws visitors, though the details of his end are debated by scholars. That is a fine thing to think about over tea in a shaded courtyard. The bazaar is a long covered street with brick vaults, packed with raisins, dried fruit, copper pots and cheap clothes.

The riding from Khoy is a matter of long, open roads across the plain, then climbs into dry mountains where the bends tighten and the surface can change from fine asphalt to patched repairs. Lorries heading to the Turkish border at Bazargan fill the main road, so patience is useful, and overtaking is a game with local rules. Roadside police checkpoints are common and usually polite. To the north the land rises toward the Aras gorge and the Armenian chapels, and to the north-west, on a clear day, the snow cone of Ararat floats above the horizon, one of the great sights of the region.

Fuel is cheap and available in the city, with stations on the ring roads and along the highways. Foreign riders in Iran need the right paperwork for a vehicle and a valid visa, so confirm the current rules well in advance rather than hoping for the best. Spring brings green fields and blossom, early autumn brings the grape harvest and warm days. Summers are dry and hot at midday, winters are bitterly cold on the plateau, and the snow can close passes quickly.
t.spas klepiki@55.1,40.2:
Meshchera is the part of Russia that writers fall in love with. It is a low, sandy, forested plain south of the Oka, full of lakes, peat bogs and pine woods, and the author Konstantin Paustovsky, who wrote lovingly of it in the 1930s, called it a land of quiet beauty with nothing spectacular about it. Spas-Klepiki is a small town of about six thousand people on the edge of this country, and the starting point for one of the oddest railways in Europe.

The Meshchera narrow-gauge line, which runs from the town into the forest, was built to haul peat and is said to be among the longest of its kind on the continent. Little diesel trains, with a few open carriages, still run along it in summer, carrying passengers through birch and pine, past lakes and clearings. Peat extraction left its mark here, and in 2010 a heatwave set off fires in the dried bogs that sent smoke across Moscow. Today the area is partly protected as the Meshchersky National Park, and the wetlands are an important refuge for birds, beavers and elk.

For riders, the roads are quiet and flat, with the pace set by the sandy soil and the trees. Surfaces are mixed: stretches of fair asphalt, and sections that crack and sink where the ground is wet. Some tracks into the forest are sand that can trap a heavy bike, so keep to the paved roads unless you know the way. Mosquitoes in summer are determined, and autumn is lovely when the birches turn gold, though rain can set in. To the north-west, the road along the Oka leads to Konstantinovo, the village where the poet Sergei Yesenin was born in 1895, and where his family house is now a museum.

Spas-Klepiki has fuel, shops and a few places to eat, but beyond it the villages are small, so top up. Foreign riders should check current conditions before planning travel.
t.chacas@-9.2,-77.4:
Chacas is a mountain town that carves its own doors. Wooden balconies, panelled doorways, carved window frames and religious statues are everywhere, and the work is not tourist craft but a living tradition taught in a school of woodwork started here by an Italian priest, Ugo de Censi, who arrived in the Andes in the 1970s and decided that young people needed a trade as much as a prayer. The result is an unusually handsome little town on a high Andean slope, with a church well worth stepping into. Yauya is the nearest larger place, about twenty kilometres off, and Carhuaz about thirty-three.

The roads in this region are made of bends. The route from Chacas climbs on its way toward the Punta Olimpica pass, winding along the side of deep valleys where small terraces of potatoes, maize and beans climb the hillsides like steps. The surface varies, with good tarmac in places and broken or gravelly patches elsewhere, and rockfalls and landslides are common in the rainy season, from about December to March. The best time to ride is the dry season, between May and September, when the skies are blue and the peaks of the Cordillera Blanca stand in sharp white lines on the horizon.

At this altitude, about three and a half thousand metres, the air is thin and cool, and a day in the sun can become a cold evening in minutes. If you have flown in from the coast, take it slowly, drink water and do not rush. Your engine will feel the lack of oxygen and lose a little of its punch, a polite reminder that you are in the real Andes. In the evening the town fills with the smoke of wood fires, the sound of church bells and a clutch of children playing football in the square.

Fuel is limited, so fill in Carhuaz or Huaraz before you climb. In Chacas you will find small restaurants and family-run guesthouses, serving hearty soups, trout, and guinea pig if you are curious. Wake early, because morning is when the mountains are clearest and the roads are quietest.
t.punta olimpica@-9.1,-77.5:
Punta Olimpica is a hole in the sky. At 4,736 metres it is one of the highest road crossings in the world, and the pass is marked by a tunnel, about a kilometre long, that cuts through the rock directly under the crest of the Cordillera Blanca. When you roll out of the far end of it, the whole range spreads before you in an astonishing line of glaciers and peaks, with Huascarán, the highest mountain in Peru, somewhere along the horizon. Carhuaz lies about twenty-four kilometres from here by road, and Yauya a bit further on the other side.

The ride is, quite simply, extreme. The road climbs from the valley floor in a series of hairpins, steep and tight, with big drop-offs and few barriers. It is paved for most of its length these days, but the surface can break up under the weight of trucks and weather, and landslides and fallen rock are frequent in the wet months. Weather is the real challenge: snow, hail and freezing fog can blow in within minutes, so go in the morning and be off the pass before the afternoon storms build. The best season is dry, from about May to September.

The altitude is the other thing to respect. Few places you can reach on a motorcycle sit this high, and the air holds about half the oxygen it does at sea level. Your bike will run rough and weak, you will feel dizzy and slow, and it is well worth spending a night or two at Huaraz or Chacas before you try it. Drink plenty of water, go slowly, and if you get a pounding headache, descend.

The scenery is otherworldly. Chilly lakes lie in glacial bowls, rough grassland called puna stretches across the slopes, and llamas and alpacas graze among the rocks. Stop at the tunnel mouth, put your gloves on and take a long look, because few views in the Andes repay the effort as generously as this one.
t.cathedral of the assumption@56.2,40.4:
Vladimir sits on a ridge above the Klyazma river, about two hours east of Moscow, and the Assumption Cathedral is the building that tells you why anyone bothered. It went up in the late 1150s under Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky, who had moved his power base out of Kiev's orbit and wanted a capital with a church to match his ambitions. After a fire in the 1180s his brother Vsevolod had the walls extended around the original core, which is why the white limestone looks bigger and stranger than a twelfth-century church has any right to. For a couple of centuries this was where the grand princes were crowned, and inside there are traces of the Last Judgement frescoes that Andrei Rublev and Daniil Chorny painted in 1408. They are faded, but the faces still look surprisingly alive.

Park on the side streets and walk. The cathedral stands on the bluff next to a small park, and from the viewing terrace you look down over the river meadows and the railway to the lowland that stretches toward Nizhny Novgorod. The Golden Gate, a triumphal arch with a defensive tower on top that dates from the 1160s, is a short stroll away. The old centre is compact, the cobbles are rough on a loaded bike, and the one-way system is a nuisance, so a morning visit before the tour buses arrive makes sense.

The riding around here is gentle central Russian country: long straight roads through birch and pine, farm villages with carved window frames, the occasional hill where a church tower pokes above the trees. Nothing technical, but the light on a summer evening is lovely, and trucks on the main Moscow to Nizhny highway can wear you down, so use the smaller roads when you can. Vladimir has a population of more than 300,000, so fuel, food and a bed are never a problem, and the ride out to Bogolyubovo, where Andrei's palace stood, takes under twenty minutes.

Local food is straightforward and honest: pickled cucumbers from Suzdal, which has a festival for them, the cherries Vladimir is known for, and mead in the tourist places. Winters are properly cold, with snow lingering into April, so the sensible riding window runs from May to September. Check current travel advice before planning a trip to Russia, because conditions for foreign visitors change quickly.
t.cathedral of st demetrius@56.1,40.4:
Vladimir has a talent for making you look at walls. The Cathedral of St Demetrius, built in the 1190s for Prince Vsevolod the Big Nest, is smaller than the Assumption Cathedral down the street, but its limestone surface is covered in carved relief, hundreds of figures: saints, griffins, lions, flowers, and in the middle of it all King David playing his harp with a crowd of animals around him. Almost nothing is repeated, and some of the stone has worn so smooth that the figures seem to be melting. Photographers love it in the late afternoon when the sun slants across the carving.

The cathedral stood in the princely court, and Vsevolod, the last great ruler of the old Vladimir principality, got his nickname from his huge family of children. The church was his private chapel. Later restorations in the nineteenth century changed some of the details, and not everyone loves the repairs, but the sculptural effect remains one of the most remarkable in medieval Russia. It is part of the same UNESCO listing as the Assumption Cathedral and the monuments of Suzdal.

The surroundings are an easy city walk: a park on the bluff, old merchants' houses, a modest museum, and cafes on the main street where you can sit and warm your hands with tea. Vladimir is a city of some three hundred thousand people, so fuel stations and food are never an issue, and the ring road gets you away from the one-way streets quickly. Traffic is heavy on weekdays, and drivers here are impatient, so a Sunday morning is a calmer time to arrive.

Beyond the city, the countryside is gentle and wooded, and the roads toward Suzdal and Bogolyubovo take you through fields, birch and meadows with onion domes in the distance. It is not twisty riding, and it is not meant to be. The point is the unhurried, slightly melancholic landscape that fed centuries of Russian painting and poetry. Summer evenings are long and warm, autumn brings colour, and winter is hard, so plan on May to September. Check the latest travel advice before planning a trip to Russia.
t.white monuments of vladimir and suzdal@5:
The phrase White Monuments sounds like a tourism slogan, but it simply describes the stone: pale local limestone, cut and laid so well that eight centuries later the churches still look as if they grew from the ground. UNESCO lists a handful of buildings across Vladimir and Suzdal, and between them they trace how a small princedom in the forest grew into the heart of medieval Russia. You find the Assumption and St Demetrius cathedrals in Vladimir, the fortified church and palace at Bogolyubovo, the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, and in Suzdal the kremlin and its cathedral.

The Nerl church deserves a detour by itself. It stands alone in a flood meadow a short walk from Bogolyubovo, a small white church with a quiet reflection in the water when the river rises in spring. Prince Andrei built it in the 1160s, supposedly in memory of his son. In summer you cross the meadow on foot through grass up to your knees, and in winter the whole scene is silent, white on white.

The road from Vladimir to Suzdal is only about thirty-five kilometres and is easy riding, with a good surface and gentle bends through farmland and small villages. Between them lies Kideksha, where the Church of Sts Boris and Gleb, from the 1150s, is among the oldest surviving stone buildings in the region. Suzdal itself is a low town of monasteries, wooden houses and orchards, with almost no modern buildings in the centre. The Spaso-Euthymius monastery has fortress walls, and the open-air museum of wooden architecture shows farm buildings and windmills moved from the surrounding villages.

Suzdal is also where Russians come for pickled cucumbers, honey mead and a weekend away from Moscow, so expect crowds in July and August and on holiday weekends. Vladimir has all the fuel and food you need, and Suzdal has plenty of small guesthouses. Mornings are best, ideally in June or September, when the light is soft and the roads are quiet. Before any trip to Russia, check current travel advice for foreign visitors.
t.plyos@57.5,41.5:
The painter Isaac Levitan came to Plyos in 1888, looking for somewhere to escape the heat and noise of Moscow, and found a small town on a bluff above the Volga where the light did exactly what he wanted. He spent three summers here, painting the river and the hills, and produced some of his best-known landscapes, including pictures of the evening calm and the birch-lined banks. The town has never forgotten it. A museum occupies the house where he lived, and the whole place has taken on a sleepy, artistic air, with a promenade, small galleries, and cafés on the water.

Plyos itself is older, going back to the fourteenth century, when a fortress stood on the hill, and the story goes that the first walls were raised against raiders on the river. A whitewashed cathedral with a green dome crowns a mound called Cathedral Hill, and the streets below are lined with wooden and stone houses from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, many with carved window frames. The Volga is wide and slow here, with a long bend and a view of wooded hills across the water, and in the evening, boats drift by on the surface. It is, honestly, a lovely place to sit and do very little.

The ride from Kostroma follows quiet roads along the river, through forests, meadows and farm villages, with some gentle bends and long views. The surface is mostly good, though some stretches show frost damage, and you should keep an eye out for livestock and cyclists. In summer, the town gets busy with day trippers from Moscow and Ivanovo, so aim for weekdays, and spring and autumn are quieter. September brings cooler air and gold light, while winter is cold and snowy.

Fuel is not available in the town itself in the way I would rely on, and the nearest sizeable town is Privolzhsk, about sixteen kilometres away, which has stations, shops and cafés. Krasnoye-na-Volge, a similar distance on the other side, is another option. In Plyos, you will find small restaurants serving river fish, pies, and tea, and a handful of guest houses, but I would book ahead in July and August.

Walk the promenade in the evening, and look across the river. You will understand why a painter stayed.
t.murom@55.6,42.0:
Murom is a city that appears in the oldest Russian chronicles, with a heroic legend attached. The chronicle of 862 mentions it as one of the towns given to Rurik's men, and it was a centre of Finno-Ugric tribes before the Slavs arrived. It stands on the high right bank of the Oka, and the river, wide and brown, curves past with floodplain meadows and pine woods on the far side. Today the city has about a hundred and twenty thousand people, with a mix of old churches, factories, and quiet streets lined with wooden houses.

Folklore gave Murom its two famous residents. The first is Ilya Muromets, the epic warrior of the Russian bylinas, who sat paralysed for thirty years before a wandering stranger healed him, and who then became the greatest of the bogatyrs, defender of Kyiv and the Russian land. His statue stands on the embankment, and the villagers of Karacharovo, nearby, still claim him as a local. The second is the story of Peter and Fevronia, a prince and a peasant woman who lived in Murom in the thirteenth century, according to tradition, and who were so devoted that they died on the same day. The Orthodox Church honours them as patron saints of marriage, and the eighth of July is celebrated as the Day of Family, Love and Fidelity.

In modern times, Murom produced Vladimir Zworykin, who was born here in 1888 and became a pioneer of electronic television in the United States. The city also has a long tradition of baking, and the local pretzel-like kalach is a regional treat.

The ride from Vladimir follows the Oka valley through forest and farmland, with gentle curves and a mostly decent surface. Traffic is moderate, with trucks on the main road, and the best seasons are May to September. Spring floods can cover the lowlands, and in winter, the road is often icy. Take care crossing the bridges, where the surface can be rough, and watch out for speed cameras on the approaches to town.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a city of this size, with several stations, supermarkets, cafés and hotels. It is a convenient place to rest, with a lively riverside promenade and a good supply of traditional Russian food. Look at the river in the evening, with the sun low. It has not changed much in a thousand years.
t.gorodets@56.6,43.5:
Gorodets claims to be older than Nizhny Novgorod across the river, and it may be right. A fortress was founded here in the twelfth century, and a story links it with the legend of Kitezh, the invisible city that sank into a lake to escape the Mongols. The old chroniclers called it Maly Kitezh, Little Kitezh, and the legend gave the town a magical aura that still clings to its image. Whatever the truth, the town was an important military point on the Volga in the Middle Ages, and was burnt and rebuilt more than once.

What it is famous for now is decoration. Gorodets painting, a style of bright folk art with roses, horses, birds and tea-table scenes, grew up in the nineteenth century on furniture, spinning wheels and wooden toys, and it is still done by local craftsmen. The town also bakes gingerbread, in carved wooden moulds, and has a quirky museum of samovars. Along the main streets stand merchant houses with elaborate carved window frames and painted shutters, a style so lavish that the tourist office has made a brand of it, the Terem houses, with bright colours and fantasy gables. It is a cheerful and rather sweet place.

The Volga here is wide and slow, held by a reservoir behind the dam at Nizhny, and the town sits on a high, steep bank. The riding on the right bank, between Nizhny Novgorod and Gorodets, is gentle, with lorries and a lot of commuter traffic near the cities, and calmer roads beyond. The surface is mostly good, and the corners are open and easy. In summer, expect heavy traffic on weekends, with Nizhny families heading for the water. Rain can come suddenly, and the wind off the river can be sharp even in July.

Fuel and food are easy. Gorodets has several stations, and the larger town of Zavolzhye is only a few kilometres away, so you can stock up on whatever you need. Cafés serve decent pies and tea, and you can buy gingerbread to take with you, although I would not promise it will survive the ride in a pannier.

Take a stroll along the main street and look up at the carved windows. It is a quiet delight.
t.chkalovsk@56.8,43.3:
Chkalovsk has been named after a pilot, and it knows it. Valery Chkalov, born in 1904 in the village of Vasilyovo on the Volga, became the most celebrated test pilot of the Soviet Union in the 1930s, and in the summer of 1937 he flew a single-engine ANT-25 non-stop from Moscow over the North Pole to Vancouver, Washington, about sixty-three hours in the air. It was a feat that made headlines around the world. Chkalov died in 1938 testing a new fighter, and the town was renamed in his honour. His house is now a museum, with a modest family home, a collection of photographs and a hall devoted to aviation, and there is a monument in the town centre.

Beyond that, the place is a quiet Volga river town of thirteen thousand people, on the left bank of the Gorky Reservoir, a few kilometres above the dam at Gorodets. The land on this side is flat and marshy, with pine and birch woods running back from the water, and the houses are mostly wooden. The reservoir spreads wide and shallow, with islands, reed beds and seabirds, and it is a favourite spot for anglers. In May, flooded meadows turn the shore into a mirror of sky.

The surrounding roads are quiet and wide, built for lorries and light traffic, with long straights and few bends. The surface is generally fair, with patches and joints, and you need to watch for animals, cyclists and the occasional tractor on the shoulder. Summer afternoons can be hot, with thunderstorms building in the evening, and autumn rain can make the roadside muddy. It is not dramatic riding, but it has a calm that suits a slow day, and you can follow the shore on small roads between villages.

For practicalities, Chkalovsk has a few petrol stations on the main roads, shops and cafés where you can eat a hot meal of soup and meat pies. If you need more choice, Zavolzhye, about seventeen kilometres away, is bigger, and the city of Nizhny Novgorod is not far. Accommodation is simple, with guest houses and a hotel.

Visit the museum if the hours suit, and stand by the water. The sky over the reservoir is wide, and it seems fitting for a pilot.
t.pastoruri@-9.9,-77.2:
Pastoruri is a glacier in the Cordillera Blanca, in Huascarán National Park, and the road to it climbs higher than most roads in Peru, ending at a car park above five thousand metres. For decades it was the most accessible glacier in the country, a place where tourists from Huaraz could walk on ice, and it has become a symbol of climate change, because its ice has retreated rapidly over recent years. The glacier you see today is smaller than the one in older photographs, but the setting, with ice, rock and sky, is still impressive, and it is worth the climb.

The ride from Catac, a village on the main road between Huaraz and Lima, follows the Pachacoto valley and then ascends through high grassland. The road is mostly paved, with some gravel sections and rough patches, and gradients are steady. Along the way, you pass bright lakes, hot springs and fields of ichu, with snowy peaks rising on every side. The altitude is the main challenge, since the air has about half the oxygen it has at sea level, and engines struggle. Mornings are clear and cold, with afternoon clouds and storms common. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time.

A fee is charged at the park entrance, and you must register. Acclimatise in Huaraz, which lies at about three thousand metres, for at least a day or two before attempting the climb, and walk slowly on the last stretch to the ice. Altitude sickness can strike anyone, and descending is the only sure remedy.

On the way up, look for the strange forest of Puya raimondii, a giant bromeliad that is the largest in the world and can reach ten metres when it flowers. The plant grows for decades, flowers once and then dies, and its tall, spiky spire is one of the most extraordinary sights in the Andes. Vicuñas graze nearby, and condors sometimes appear. The mountains here include Huascarán, the highest in Peru, rising to nearly seven thousand metres. Pastoruri is a reminder that glaciers are not permanent, and that some things are best seen while they last.
t.caraz@-9.0,-77.8:
Caraz is a small, sunny town at the northern end of the Callejón de Huaylas, the long valley that runs between the Cordillera Blanca and the lower Cordillera Negra, and it is one of the pleasantest bases in the Peruvian Andes. The town sits at about 2,250 metres, where the air is mild and the sky usually clear, and its low houses and quiet plaza look up to a wall of snow peaks, among them Huandoy and Huascarán, both above six thousand metres. The Santa River runs through the valley, and orchards and fields cover the lower slopes.

The ride along the valley from Huaraz is a delight. The road is paved, with long, easy bends, and follows the river past small towns and farms, with the white peaks standing above to the east. Yungay, a town of about five thousand people, lies twelve kilometres to the south and has a sombre history. In 1970 an earthquake triggered an enormous avalanche from the slopes of Huascarán, burying the old town and killing tens of thousands of people, and the site is now a memorial. Carhuaz, a similar-sized town, lies further south.

Caraz has fuel, shops, restaurants, hotels and a friendly market, and it is a good place to stop for a few days if you want to explore. It is known for its sweets, especially manjar blanco, a thick milk caramel sold in small jars, and for the honey and fruit grown in the valley. Try the local trout, fresh from mountain streams, with potatoes and chilli sauce. The plaza is a good place to sit in the evening, when families take their walk and the mountains turn pink.

The valley has long been a crossroads. Before the Incas, the region was home to the Recuay culture, whose stone sculptures and tombs are still being studied, and the colonial history is evident in the churches and houses of the old centre. Nature is the main attraction, with lakes such as Laguna Parón, a turquoise lake beneath a ring of peaks, and Llanganuco within easy reach. Early morning is the best time to see the mountains, before the clouds gather. It is a gentle base for a high adventure.
t.llanganuco@-9.1,-77.6:
The Llanganuco lakes, Chinancocha and Orconcocha, lie in a steep glacial valley in Huascarán National Park at about 3,850 metres, and their colour, a deep, shining turquoise, is one of the great sights of the Peruvian Andes. Sheer walls of granite and ice rise on all sides, with the twin peaks of Huascarán, the highest mountain in Peru, to the south and the pyramid of Pisco and the massive Huandoy to the north. The names come from Quechua, and they are often explained as the female and male lakes, with Chinancocha the lower and more tranquil of the pair.

The road from Yungay, about thirteen kilometres to the west, is a classic. It leaves the valley floor and climbs steadily up a narrow gorge, then begins a series of hairpins that carry the track past the lakes and up toward the high pass above. The surface is gravel, narrow and rough, with loose stones, washboard and sheer drops in places, so ride slowly and give way to buses and trucks. Fog and rain can come in quickly, and the road can be badly damaged in the wet season. The dry months from May to September are the most reliable, and mornings are usually the clearest.

You must pay a fee at the park entrance, and the rangers will tell you about any restrictions. Altitude is again a factor, so give yourself time to adjust if you have come up quickly from the coast, and avoid exertion on arrival. A few stalls near the lakes sell hot drinks and snacks in the high season.

The scenery draws walkers and climbers from all over the world, and the lakes are the starting point for several treks. Vegetation here includes the polylepis, a tree whose red, papery bark is among the highest-growing in the world, and the forests that survive on the slopes shelter hummingbirds and Andean birds. In the evening, when the wind drops and the light turns gold, the lakes seem to glow from within. It is a remarkable place to pause on a ride through the high Andes.
t.segment qn hh 051 inca misana@-9.1,-77.2:
Five hundred years ago a runner could have passed this spot carrying a knotted quipu or a message for the governor in Huánuco Pampa, handing it on at the next post in a relay that crossed the Andes faster than a horse. This short stretch, catalogued as segment QÑ-HH-051 near Inca Misana, is a fragment of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that linked an empire from southern Colombia to central Chile. The whole network was listed by UNESCO in 2014 across six countries, and what you find on the ground here in Ancash is often modest: a line of stone paving, a retaining wall, a set of steps cut into a slope, running across high grassland with the mountains standing all around.

The setting is the Callejón de Conchucos, the long valley system on the eastern side of the Cordillera Blanca, the highest tropical mountain range in the world. The town of Yauya lies about twelve kilometres away, and Pomabamba, with its hot springs, further north. This is a land of small farms, terraced fields of potatoes and maize, eucalyptus groves and adobe villages, with Quechua the everyday language for many people. The altitude here is well above three thousand metres, and the air is thin and clear.

Riding in the Conchucos is an adventure in the full sense. Some main roads have been paved in recent years, but many routes are still gravel or dirt, with steep climbs, long drops, hairpins without barriers, landslides in the rainy season and sudden encounters with livestock, trucks and buses. Crossing from the Callejón de Huaylas over the Cordillera Blanca, through passes over four thousand metres, gives some of the most spectacular views in South America, of glaciers, turquoise lakes and peaks over six thousand metres.

Plan carefully. Fuel is available in the larger towns, but quality varies, and pumps can run dry, so carry spare fuel. The thin air reduces engine power and affects riders too, so acclimatise for a few days in Huaraz or a similar town before tackling the high passes. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time to ride. Take warm clothes, as nights are cold, and be ready to ask for help: people in the valleys are generally welcoming.
t.chavin@-9.6,-77.2:
Three thousand years ago, priests at Chavín de Huántar led pilgrims into a labyrinth of dark stone galleries beneath a temple, where at the heart of the maze stood a carved granite pillar, the Lanzón, depicting a fanged deity. The Chavín culture, flourishing between roughly 1200 and 500 BC, spread its art and religious ideas across much of the Andes, and its temple complex in the Mosna valley is one of the most important archaeological sites in South America, inscribed by UNESCO in 1985. Look out for the cabezas clavas, carved stone heads that once projected from the temple walls, showing a transformation from human to jaguar or bird.

The site sits in a deep valley on the eastern side of the Cordillera Blanca, the highest tropical mountain range in the world, and the journey there is spectacular. From Huaraz, the road climbs past Catac and the Laguna Querococha, a turquoise lake beneath glaciated peaks, before entering a tunnel at around 4,500 metres and descending steeply into the Conchucos valleys on the other side. The town of Chavín, small and friendly, sits beside the ruins and has a modern museum displaying many of the original carvings.

The road from Huaraz is paved but narrow, with tight hairpins, steep gradients and spectacular drops, and it is often affected by landslides and rockfalls in the rainy season from December to March. The altitude is a serious consideration, both for you and your bike: give yourself time to acclimatise in Huaraz before riding, carry water and warm clothing, and expect your engine to feel noticeably weaker at altitude. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time to ride, with clear skies and mountain views.

Huaraz, about forty kilometres away as the crow flies but much further by road, is the main base, with fuel, mechanics, hotels and restaurants. Fill up before you leave and do not count on finding fuel along the road. Chavín town has simple restaurants serving trout and local dishes, and a couple of guesthouses for those who want to stay the night.
t.segment canrash torrepampa@-8.9,-77.3:
The Inca road network, the Qhapaq Ñan, once linked an empire stretching from Colombia to Chile, and this segment, between Canrash and Torrepampa, runs through the high valleys of the Conchucos region in Ancash, east of the Cordillera Blanca. The Inca road here was a stone-paved trail, with steps, retaining walls and drainage channels, built for runners, soldiers and llama caravans rather than wheels. Much of it survives, winding along hillsides above the river valleys, and it is part of the transnational World Heritage listing for the Andean road system.

The landscape is spectacular and remote: steep, terraced hillsides, small villages of adobe houses, fields of potatoes and maize, and the snowy peaks of the Cordillera Blanca rising to the west. Yauya and Pomabamba are the nearest towns, both small and friendly, with Quechua spoken alongside Spanish. Local markets sell potatoes in dozens of varieties, cheese, and textiles, and the people still farm the land much as their ancestors did, with terraces, irrigation channels and communal work.

Riding here is an adventure. The roads in the Conchucos valleys are a mix of paved and unpaved, often narrow, with steep drops, tight bends and loose surfaces, and they are frequently affected by landslides in the rainy season from December to March. The altitude is considerable, with high passes and towns between 3,000 and 4,000 metres, so acclimatisation is essential. Traffic is light, mostly local buses, trucks and the occasional car, and the views are stunning. The dry season, from May to September, is the time to come.

Fuel is scarce, available in Pomabamba and a few other towns, sometimes only from drums, so carry extra and fill up whenever you can. Food is simple: soups, rice, potatoes and guinea pig on special occasions. Accommodation is basic in the small towns. Carry water, warm clothing and spare parts, and be prepared for slow, demanding riding through some of the most beautiful mountain scenery in the Andes.
t.segment otutococha qn hh 051@-9.1,-77.2:
East of the Cordillera Blanca, in the region of Ancash known as the Conchucos, the Inca road system, the Qhapaq Ñan, crossed some of the most rugged terrain of its entire network. This segment, near the small town of Yauya, is part of the main road that ran north from Cusco to Quito through the high Andes, linking administrative centres such as Huánuco Pampa to the south. The Inca engineers laid stone paving, built steps on steep slopes, retaining walls and drainage channels, and stretches of the road can still be walked today, threading across high grasslands and past lakes at altitudes well over three and a half thousand metres. The whole network, which crosses six countries, became a World Heritage site in 2014.

The landscape is enormous. The valleys drop steeply towards the Marañón River in the east, terraced fields cling to the slopes, and above, the grasslands of the puna stretch to rocky peaks. The weather changes quickly; the dry season, roughly from May to September, brings clear skies and cold nights, while the rainy season turns the tracks into mud and causes landslides. The light at this altitude is very bright, and the sun burns quickly.

Riding here is a serious undertaking. From Huaraz, the road crosses the Cordillera Blanca through the Punta Olímpica tunnel, one of the highest road tunnels in the world, with spectacular views of the glaciers on the way, then descends towards Chacas and San Luis. Other routes pass through Chavín de Huántar, with its ancient temple complex, essential for anyone interested in Andean history. Roads in the Conchucos are a mixture of new asphalt and dirt, with unprotected edges, landslides and few other vehicles. Altitude affects both rider and engine; take it slowly, drink coca tea, and plan for cold.

Fuel is available in the larger towns such as Huaraz, Chavín, San Luis and Pomabamba, but not always at the smaller ones, and it is wise to carry extra. Yauya has basic shops and lodging. The local food is hearty: soups with potatoes and quinoa, roasted guinea pig on special occasions, and fresh trout from the mountain lakes. Above all, respect the communities through which the road passes; it is still their road.
t.segment huanuco pampa huaricashash@-9.8,:
Three and a half thousand metres up, on the cold grass plateau of the Peruvian Andes, the Incas built a city that was never meant to be a home. Huánuco Pampa was an administrative centre, a stop on the great road between Cusco and Quito, with a vast central plaza, an ushnu platform from which officials presided over ceremonies, rows of long halls for visitors and hundreds of storehouses lined up on the hillsides. The people who staffed it were moved in from elsewhere, and the labour they owed was paid in cloth, maize and llama wool that fed the road and the army.

The road itself is the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca network of roughly thirty thousand kilometres linking the empire's provinces, of which UNESCO listed a selection in 2014. This segment runs from the ruins towards Huaricashash, and in places you can still follow the paved surface, the stone drains, and the retaining walls that held it against the mountain. The engineering is the lesson: steps where the slope was steep, causeways across boggy ground, bridges woven from grass across the gorges. Nothing was built for wheels, because the Incas had none, and the road was walked and used by llama trains.

For a rider, the access is the adventure. The nearest town on our list is La Unión, a small highland place in the Dos de Mayo province, and from there the way to the ruins is on unpaved mountain tracks that are rough, narrow and sometimes washed out. The altitude means thin air, cold nights and sudden weather, and from December to March the rains make the tracks slick and dangerous. The dry season, from May to September, is much better, with intense sun by day and frost at night. Carry warm layers, because the plateau is exposed, and take it slowly.

Bring food and water as well, because services near the ruins are minimal, and a local guide from the nearby villages is well worth finding. Altitude sickness is real up here, so give yourself a day to acclimatise, and drink coca tea if it is offered.
On a bare hillside near the border between Iran and Turkey, close to the foot of Mount Ararat, stands a black-and-white church that has survived earthquakes, wars and neglect for most of a thousand years. The Monastery of Saint Thaddeus, known in Iran as Qara Kelisa, the Black Church, is one of the oldest and most revered Armenian churches in the world. It is built of alternating bands of black and white stone, in a way that gives it a striking, almost chequered appearance, and it stands in a high, windy valley of the north-west.

According to tradition, the monastery was founded on the site where the apostle Thaddeus, one of the early missionaries to Armenia, was martyred in the first century. A church has stood here since the early centuries of Christianity, though the present building mostly dates from the fourteenth century, after an earthquake damaged an earlier one, and the dome was rebuilt in the nineteenth century. UNESCO listed the Armenian monastic ensembles of Iran in 2008, and this is the main one. Every July, Armenians from Iran and elsewhere gather here for a pilgrimage with mass, processions and a communal meal, and it is an exceptional moment to visit.

The road to it passes through high, empty country of volcanic hills, grazing land and small villages, with a sense of space and the mountains of eastern Turkey visible in the distance. The nearest towns are Maku, a town in a dramatic rocky gorge, and the small settlements near the border. Roads in the region are generally good main routes, but side roads can be rough, and winter brings heavy snow and bitter cold, closing some of them, so late spring to early autumn is the best time. Be prepared for border-zone checkpoints, and carry your passport and permits at all times.

Fuel and food are available in Maku, and in the small villages along the road you can find simple meals, bread, yoghurt and tea. Dress modestly, especially in the church, and ask before photographing people. The best time to visit is in the early morning, when the light on the black-and-white stone is soft and the hills are quiet, and the place feels as if it has not changed for centuries.
t.segment inka hamash ayash@-9.5,-77.0:
The high Andes of central Peru are less visited than the Cusco region, but the Incas were here too, and the old royal road, the Qhapaq Nan, runs through the mountains of Huanuco Region, with segments surviving in the hills above the towns of Llata and La Union. The Inka Hamash to Ayash segment lies in this remote country, with Llata about twenty-five kilometres away, and I cannot say what you will see at the point on your map, but I can describe the world that surrounds it.

The Qhapaq Nan was a network of roads that linked the empire from Colombia to Chile, over thirty thousand kilometres in all, with relay stations, storehouses and bridges. The segment listed here is part of a branch that connected Huanuco Pampa, one of the main Inca administrative centres in the northern highlands, with the main road to Cusco. The paths are usually paved with flat stones, with steps on steep sections and low walls on the edge, and many are still in use by farmers and herders who walk them with llamas and donkeys. Rope suspension bridges, rebuilt every year in some places, are an Inca technology that survives.

The country is rugged and beautiful. From the Marañón river valley the road climbs through terraced fields of potatoes, quinoa and barley, to cold grassland above three thousand metres, with snow peaks of the Cordillera Blanca and Huayhuash to the west. The roads are often dirt, steep and narrow, with sheer drops and landslides in the rainy season from November to March, so this is a place for experienced riders on suitable bikes. The dry months of June to September are best. At that height, mornings are freezing, the sun is fierce, and afternoon clouds bring hail or rain, so layers and waterproofs are essential. Altitude sickness is a real risk if you arrive from the coast.

Services are few. Llata, with about four and a half thousand people, and La Union, with a similar number, have small shops, a few simple restaurants and basic lodging, and fuel is sold in small quantities, so fill up whenever you see a pump, and carry extra. Try a hearty bowl of soup, trout from the highland streams, and a cup of coca tea, which helps with the altitude. Carry cash in soles, because cards are rare, and tell someone where you are going.
t.segment huaricashash isco@-9.8,-76.9:
La Union is a small market town in a high valley of the Huanuco Region, in the central Peruvian Andes, and the Huaricashash to Isco segment lies about eleven kilometres from it, in a landscape of steep terraced hillsides, eucalyptus groves and distant snow peaks. It is the same Inca road network as the neighbouring segments, but this stretch sits close to the greatest Inca site in the region.

Huanuco Pampa, an Inca city on a high plateau at about 3,700 metres, was built in the late fifteenth century as an administrative centre on the royal road from Cusco to Quito. It was laid out around a vast central plaza, with a platform at its heart, the ushnu, where the Inca ruler or his representative would watch ceremonies. Around it stood hundreds of storehouses, workshops and barracks, with room to house thousands of people at a time, and the surviving stone walls, the trapezoid doorways and the sheer scale tell you how much labour the empire could command. Local communities sent workers to serve in the city under the labour system called the mita, and the storehouses held maize, textiles and weapons. The site is wide, windswept and almost empty today, and it is a magnificent place to walk on a clear day.

The road from La Union runs through the high puna, a landscape of yellow ichu grass, small lakes and herds of llamas and alpacas, with no trees and a huge sky. The dirt roads are rough and sometimes closed by rain or landslides, with streams to ford and stretches of loose rock, and the altitude brings freezing nights, so it is not a trip for the faint-hearted. Mist, hail and sudden storms occur even in the dry season, and thunder rolls around the hills in the afternoon. The best months are June to August, and in the rainy season, from December to March, routes can be impassable.

La Union has a few shops, a market, basic lodging and places that serve hot soup and fried trout. Fuel is limited, so buy it in Huanuco or in La Union itself and carry some extra. Take warm clothing, a hat for the sun, plenty of water and a good map, and ask local people about the state of the road before you set off.
t.segment taulli tambillo@-9.4,-77.1:
In the high valleys of Huánuco, north of Lima and east of the great white wall of the Cordillera Blanca, an Inca road crosses a landscape of stone-walled fields and thatched farms. The Qhapaq Ñan ran north from Cusco to Quito by way of an inland route, and one of its major administrative centres was Huánuco Pampa, a vast planned town on a plateau at about 3,700 metres, with a great plaza, storehouses and barracks, where the emperor's officials gathered tribute and fed travelling armies. Segments of the road around Llata, in the Huamalíes province, connect with that old network. The name Taulli Tambillo suggests a tambo, a small way station of the sort that stood every day's walk along the road, and I do not know the specific site, so I will say only that the labels point to a stretch of trail between a pass and a village.

Llata sits in the Marañón basin, in a countryside of steep valleys, potato fields and eucalyptus, with peaks above and canyons below.
