The Marañón, one of the main sources of the Amazon, has cut a deep slot through the Andes here, and the roads that approach it drop thousands of metres in a few hours. This is a quiet part of Peru, with few tourists and warm hospitality, and farmers selling cheese and potatoes at small markets.

The riding is demanding. The roads in Huánuco are a mix of paved highway and rough track, with narrow bends over sheer drops, and rain turns the surface to mud quickly. The dry season from May to September is the time to go. Daytime can be warm, but nights at altitude are near freezing, and fog rolls in during the afternoons. Altitude sickness is possible at the passes, so go slowly.

Fuel is limited. Llata is a town of a few thousand people and I cannot promise a station, so fill the tank in Huánuco or Tingo María before heading to the high roads, and bring a spare can. Food is simple and hearty, with trout soup, roasted guinea pig, and plates of rice, potatoes and beans.

Walk a few hundred metres of the old stone road, if you find it, and feel the care with which the stones were laid, still firm after five hundred years.
t.segment escalerilla casa blanca cerro h@:
Huamachuco is a big market town in the highlands of La Libertad, at about 3,200 metres, and it has been an important place for much longer than the Incas. On the hills above the town, the ruins of Marcahuamachuco spread across a long ridge, with huge stone walls and galleries that were raised during the first millennium AD, in a culture that flourished at the same time as the Wari empire and ruled the northern highlands. A big part of the stonework still stands, including a long building called the Castillo, with three storeys of stone galleries. The Incas arrived much later, in the fifteenth century, and ran their road system through the area, and parts of the Qhapaq Ñan around Huamachuco are among those listed by UNESCO in 2014.

The road segments in the ride titles, with the names Escalerilla and Casa Blanca, are local places, and I do not know exactly what sits at each, so I will describe the country around them. This is a landscape of high puna and cultivated slopes, with eucalyptus plantations, fields of potatoes and quinoa and herds of cattle. To the north, the mining town of Quiruvilca sits at close to 4,000 metres in a bleak, rocky zone with copper and silver workings that have been dug for centuries.

For a rider, it is a good region to explore, though not an easy one. The road from Trujillo on the coast climbs in a great arc from the desert to the highlands, passing through different climates in a few hours, from dry coast to cold mist, and there is a gravel section on some of the routes. Landslides in the wet season from December to March can block roads, and the cold on the highlands is real, so carry layers and waterproofs. The dry months from May to September give clear skies and chilly nights.

Huamachuco is a lively market town with some twenty thousand inhabitants, and it has fuel, hotels and simple restaurants, so it makes the natural base. Quiruvilca, with nine thousand people, may have fuel but would be a risky bet. I would fill up in Huamachuco before heading to the high roads.

Try a plate of cuy, the local guinea pig, or a hot soup with potatoes and cheese on a cold evening, and ask in the plaza about the way to the ruins, because the locals are proud of them.
t.kremlin of suzdal and cathedral of the n:
Cucumbers are the unlikely stars of Suzdal. Every July the town holds a festival in their honour, with pickles sold from barrels, cucumber-themed games and a great deal of vodka, and the joke only works because the place is otherwise so solemn. Suzdal, a town of about eleven thousand people on the Kamenka river, in the Vladimir region some two hundred kilometres east of Moscow, is a museum of old Russia: onion domes, white-stone churches, wooden houses with carved window frames, meadows running down to the river, and almost no modern buildings of any size. It is part of the Golden Ring of towns that grew up around Moscow, and the white monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal were listed by UNESCO in 1992.

At the centre is the Kremlin, which is more a fortified compound than a fortress, with an earthen rampart, a bishop's palace and the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Virgin. The cathedral's blue domes, covered in gold stars, stand out against the sky, and the lower walls hold the oldest part of the building, white stone from the early thirteenth century, with gilded doors of the same age. Inside, painted frescoes cover the walls and ceiling in deep colour. Suzdal was a capital of its own principality for a time, and a centre of pilgrimage, with dozens of churches and monasteries tucked among the houses.

For a rider, this is gentle country. The roads across the flat farmland of the Vladimir region are fairly straight, with long views over fields, birch woods and villages, and the main route from Moscow to Vladimir and Suzdal is a busy highway with heavy lorry traffic. The surface can be rutted, especially after winter, so watch for frost damage. The better stretch is the quiet road from Vladimir to Suzdal, about thirty-five kilometres, which passes through fields and small villages. In summer the long evenings are warm and bright, in October the birches turn yellow, and in winter the snow gives the white churches a fairy-tale look, though the roads are icy.

The ride goes on to the Golden Gate in Vladimir, a twelfth-century defensive gate topped with a small church, which stands at the entrance to the old city. Suzdal has small fuel stations on the approach roads, and Vladimir, a much larger city, has everything. Do not leave without trying medovukha, the local honey mead, and a plate of pickled mushrooms, and the town's restaurants serve filling dishes like pelmeni and sour cabbage soup. The pace is slow, and that is part of the charm.
t.the main chapel@39.2,44.5:
Black and white stone, in alternating courses, climbs the walls of a church that stands alone on a hillside in the far north-west of Iran. The Armenians call it the monastery of Saint Thaddeus, and the Persians know it as Qara Kelisa, the black church, a name that comes from the dark stone of its lower walls. Tradition says that a chapel was founded here in the first century by the apostle Thaddeus, who was martyred nearby, and that this makes it one of the oldest places of Christian worship in the world. The buildings that stand today are mostly of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, rebuilt after an earthquake, and they are among the finest examples of Armenian architecture outside Armenia.

The setting is a high, treeless valley in West Azerbaijan province, with rolling brown hills, small fields and the occasional shepherd. Mount Ararat is not far to the north, and on a clear day you may see its snowy cone across the border in Turkey. The main chapel is built in a restrained, powerful style, with a conical dome and carved stone around the doors, and inside it is cool, plain and silent. The monastery is on UNESCO's list of Armenian Monastic Ensembles of Iran, inscribed in 2008.

Every year, in July, Armenians from Iran and abroad make a pilgrimage here, and for a few days the place fills with people, food and singing. At other times, it can be a very quiet spot, with just a caretaker. If you visit, dress modestly, and ask before photographing inside.

Riding in this part of the country is demanding. The roads are mostly paved but narrow, winding and sometimes broken, and weather at this altitude shifts fast, with snow likely from late autumn through spring. The nearest large town is Maku, which has fuel and places to eat, and you should not count on finding any near the monastery itself. Travel rules for foreigners in Iran, especially with a motorcycle, are complicated, so check them well in advance and carry all paperwork. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.the village@39.1,44.5:
The village near the black church is a world of mud, stone and apricot trees. Low houses with flat roofs are built into the slope, with piles of fuel cakes drying against the walls, smoke curling from chimneys in the evening, and the sound of sheep and dogs echoing in the valley. People here live much as they have for generations, growing grain and fruit, herding animals and trading with the markets in the towns below. This corner of West Azerbaijan is a mix of Azeri and Kurdish villages, with Armenian history layered underneath.

Visiting is a matter of manners. A motorcycle is an event, and children and older men will probably gather as soon as you stop. Greet people, accept tea if it is offered, and ask before taking photographs. Hospitality in Iran is a serious matter and can be overwhelming, and a few words of Persian go a long way. Women riders should follow the local dress rules and carry a headscarf.

The land around is high, open and dry, with hills the colour of toast, spring flowers that appear briefly in May, and a wide sky. In summer the days are hot and the nights are cool. In winter the area is cold and snowy, and roads can close. The monastery of Saint Thaddeus is on its hillside not far away, and the village is the human side of the same story: the people who have lived beside the church for centuries, whatever the religion of the day.

The roads leading in are paved but patched, and some stretches are narrow, with sharp curves and drops. Watch for livestock, slow trucks and potholes, and for the occasional unmarked speed bump. Fuel is not available in the village itself, so fill up in Maku or another larger town on the main road, and carry some spare. Mobile coverage can be patchy.

The best times to come are late spring and early autumn, when the air is clear and warm. Bring food and water, and allow plenty of time for conversation. Travel permissions for foreigners in Iran can be complicated, so check them well before you leave.
t.suzdal@56.4,40.4:
Suzdal is a small town on the Kamenka river, in the Russian heartland north-east of Moscow, and it is a place where the Russia of old churches and wooden houses survives almost whole. With a population of about eleven thousand, it has more than two dozen churches, five monasteries and a kremlin, all packed into a few square kilometres of low green meadows and willow-lined streams, and no factory chimney or tower block disturbs the skyline. The town was first mentioned in a chronicle of 1024, and for a time in the twelfth century it was the capital of the principality, until power shifted to Vladimir and later Moscow, leaving Suzdal a quiet backwater. That is exactly why it survived intact.

The buildings are the draw. The Kremlin, a walled enclosure on a bend of the river, has the Nativity Cathedral, with blue domes dotted with gold stars and portals decorated in white stone carving from the thirteenth century. The Monastery of Saint Euthymius, which doubled as a prison for political prisoners under the Tsars, has high fortress walls and a bell tower that rings at noon. The Pokrovsky Convent, founded in the fourteenth century, was the place where Tsars sent unwanted wives. Together with the monuments of nearby Vladimir, the town has been on the UNESCO list since 1992. There is also an open-air museum of wooden architecture, with windmills and log churches moved here from surrounding villages, which is delightful in winter under snow.

The local food and drink are an attraction in themselves. Suzdal is famous for its pickled cucumbers, celebrated in an annual festival, and for medovukha, a honey mead often served warm, along with horseradish and the thick sour cream of the region. Fresh bread and honey are sold in the market, and little restaurants serve hearty soups and dumplings.

For riders, the roads around Suzdal are gentle, passing through flat farmland, birch and pine woods and villages with carved wooden window frames. The surface can be patchy, with potholes after winter, and the old road to Vladimir, about thirty-five kilometres away, is busy with lorries. Early summer and early autumn are the best seasons, with long light and the smell of hay or woodsmoke. Fuel is available in Suzdal and in Vladimir, which is the larger city, and it is wise to check the current situation for travel and fuel before planning a trip.
t.bogolyubovo@56.2,40.5:
Bogolyubovo is a small village on the River Klyazma, about ten kilometres east of Vladimir, and it carries one of the most beautiful small buildings in Russia. The Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, built in 1165, stands alone in a flood meadow where the little Nerl River meets the Klyazma, a slender, white limestone church with a single dome, rising above the water on a raised mound. The walls are carved with figures, lions and delicate arcading, and the proportions are so perfect that the building seems to float. In spring, when the meadow floods, it is reflected in the water.

It was built by Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky, who moved the political centre of northern Russia from Kiev to Vladimir and made his residence here, in a fortified palace at Bogolyubovo, from which the village takes its name. Tradition says that he raised the church in memory of his son, who died in battle. In 1174, Andrei was murdered in his palace by conspirators from among his own boyars, and the stairway tower where the murder occurred still survives as part of the later monastery. The Bogolyubsky Monastery next door, with its white walls and green domes, was founded on the site of the old palace.

Together with the white-stone monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal, the church is part of a UNESCO World Heritage site, and it is a place of peace. To reach it from the road, you walk for about a kilometre across the meadow along a path through tall grass, with wildflowers in early summer and the smell of damp earth and hay. In the evening, the light is golden and the church glows, and in winter the snow gives it a stark, quiet look. Swallows nest in the eaves.

The village is small, so fuel and services are best found in Vladimir, a city of over three hundred thousand people, ten kilometres away, with stations, restaurants and hotels. The road from there is flat and easy, with the old highway running along the river, and traffic is moderate. Parking at the meadow is simple, but the path can be muddy after rain, so bring sensible boots. Mosquitoes can be annoying in summer. A bowl of hot soup and tea in a local cafe makes a good end to the visit.
t.portachuelo de llanganuco@-9.0,-77.6:
The Portachuelo de Llanganuco is a notch in the ridge of the Cordillera Blanca at 4,767 metres, and the road that climbs to it, a gravel track of tight switchbacks, is one of the high points of any Peruvian ride, in every sense. It runs from the valley of the Santa river, past two lakes, and up a steep, bare slope to a pass between giant peaks. From the top, the view is of glaciers and snowfields, and the great mass of Huascarán, at 6,768 metres the highest mountain in Peru, looms to the south. The air is thin, the wind is cold and the sky is an extraordinary deep blue.

The pass lies in Huascarán National Park, a World Heritage Site, and the mountains around it are among the most heavily glaciated in the tropics. The glaciers are retreating fast, and a visit is a reminder of how much is changing. At the bottom of the valley lies Yungay, a town with a tragic past: in 1970, an earthquake shook an enormous mass of ice and rock from the north face of Huascarán, and the avalanche buried the old town, killing thousands. The site is now a memorial, and the new town was built nearby. It is worth a quiet visit.

The ride is a serious one. The road is gravel, steep and narrow, with sharp hairpins and big drops, and the surface is often loose, rutted or wet. At 4,700 metres, the engine loses power, and the rider loses concentration, so go slowly and rest often. Altitude sickness is a real risk, with headaches, nausea and shortness of breath, so spend a few days at altitude in Huaraz first, drink water and descend if you feel unwell. Weather changes fast, and snow and hail are possible at any time of year. The road is best ridden in the dry season, from May to September, in the morning.

Yungay, about eighteen kilometres below, has a few stations, and Caraz and Huaraz have more, so start with a full tank. A small entrance fee is charged for the national park, so carry some cash. Take warm clothing, sun protection and plenty of water, and be prepared to turn back if the weather closes in. The view from the top is among the finest on the continent, and it is earned.
t.llanganuco lakes@-9.1,-77.6:
The Llanganuco lakes are two glacial lakes at about 3,850 metres, in a deep, U-shaped valley below the great peaks of the Cordillera Blanca, and their colour is out of this world. The lower lake, Chinancocha, is a deep turquoise, and the upper one, Orconcocha, is a darker green, and both shine with a milky intensity that comes from finely ground rock suspended in the glacier-fed water. Steep slopes of rock and polylepis forest, a tough, twisted tree that grows higher than any other in the world, rise on either side, and the snowy summits of Huandoy and Pisco crown the valley. The names come from Quechua: Chinancocha is the female lake, and Orconcocha the male.

The valley is part of Huascarán National Park, and it is a place of extraordinary beauty. Mist rises from the water in the morning, the wind ruffles the surface, and in the afternoon the light turns the glaciers pink and gold. Andean birds live here, and with luck you may see a vizcacha, a rabbit-like rodent, sitting on a rock. Rangers collect a small entrance fee at the gate, and you should carry cash.

The road from Yungay is gravel for much of its length, climbing steadily from the valley, with bends, bumps and a few steep sections. It is a rough, dusty ride, but the surface is not too difficult, and the gradient is gentle compared with the road above the lakes. Rain can make it slippery, and landslides sometimes block it, so check conditions. Because the lakes lie at nearly 3,900 metres, the air is thin, and a rider coming from the coast may feel breathless. Take it slowly, rest, and drink water, ideally after a few days of getting used to the height.

Fuel is available in Yungay, about thirteen kilometres away, and Caraz and Huaraz have more. Boats are sometimes available to take visitors out on the water. Cold wind comes off the glaciers, so bring a windproof layer, a hat and gloves. Go early, before the clouds gather, and take the time to walk to the shore, where the water laps against the stones and the quiet comes down around you.
t.huaraz@-9.5,-77.5:
Huaraz sits at about three thousand metres in the Callejon de Huaylas, a long, high valley between the Cordillera Blanca and the Cordillera Negra in the Peruvian Andes. The Cordillera Blanca rises along the east side, white with glaciers, and holds the highest tropical mountains in the world, including Huascaran, which at 6,768 metres is the highest peak in Peru. On a clear morning the whole range shows over the roofs of the town, an almost unreal wall of ice. Huaraz was largely destroyed in the great earthquake of 1970, which killed tens of thousands across the region and buried the nearby town of Yungay under an avalanche from Huascaran. The modern town is mostly new, a busy, practical place for trekkers and climbers.

A circuit around Huascaran is one of the great high-altitude rides. Roads from Huaraz run north along the valley, past Carhuaz and Yungay, then climb to the Llanganuco lakes, where emerald water lies under the glaciers, and over the high pass of Portachuelo, at about 4,700 metres, toward the eastern side of the range. Roads are mostly paved in the valley, but side roads are steep and rough. Altitude is the real adversary: the air is thin, the bike loses power, and a rider can feel dizzy or headachy. Take a day or two to acclimatise in Huaraz before climbing high, drink water, and go slowly.

The weather follows a clear pattern. The dry season, from May to September, brings sunny days and cold nights, and it is the best time for riding and trekking. The wet season, from December to March, brings rain, snow on the passes and cloud that hides the peaks. Temperatures drop fast after sunset, and frost is common on the high roads.

Huaraz is the place to stock up. It has fuel, a large market, plenty of restaurants and guesthouses, and shops that rent gear. Carhuaz, thirty kilometres north, is a smaller town with basic supplies, and beyond it services thin out. Local food runs to trout from the lakes, roasted guinea pig, and a hearty soup called caldo de gallina. The pachamanca, a meal of meat and potatoes cooked in a pit with hot stones, is a regional speciality. Coca tea is offered everywhere, and many find it helps with the altitude.
t.chankillo@-9.6,-78.2:
Chankillo stands in the desert of Peru's northern coast, in the valley of Casma, and it is among the most puzzling ancient sites in the Americas. Here, more than two thousand years ago, people built a vast ceremonial complex on a barren plain: a hilltop fortress of concentric walls, a temple, plazas and a long ridge of towers. The people who raised it lived in the early centuries before the Inca and long before the Spanish, and their culture left no writing. The complex is a UNESCO site, and it is regarded as one of the oldest solar observatories in the Americas.

The country around is stark. The Pan-American Highway runs through a desert of sand and rock, with irrigated green valleys cutting across it where rivers descend from the Andes. Between the valleys, the plain is empty and brown, and the wind is steady, carrying fine sand across the road. Riding here is mostly long, straight, flat running with a strong crosswind, and the main hazard is trucks overtaking on blind rises. In the early morning, a low sea mist often covers the coast, and then burns off by late morning.

The fortified temple is the biggest structure, a stone building of three concentric walls and many gates, laid out like a maze. Archaeologists debate whether it was a fortress or a ceremonial centre. The walls are partly restored, and from the highest point you can see across the plain to the towers. Walking the site takes an hour or two, and there is little shade, so bring a hat, sun protection and plenty of water.

The nearest large town is Casma, on the coast, where you will find fuel, simple restaurants and places to sleep. It is known for fresh seafood, particularly ceviche, which is served with sweet potato and toasted corn. Further along the coast, Huarmey and Chimbote have more services. The best season is from April to December, when the weather is dry and the days are bright, though the coastal desert is always dry. Summers, between January and March, are hot.

This is a place for those who like to walk slowly through the past, under a wide sky, and puzzle at what its builders were thinking.
t.chankillo archaeoastronomical complex@-9:
At Chankillo, the thing to look for is the line of thirteen towers on the ridge. They stand in a row along a low hill, each about two to six metres tall, spaced almost evenly like the teeth of a comb, and from a distance they look like a set of stone fingers. They date to the fourth or third century BC, and they are the key to the site's fame. Researchers have shown that if you stand at the right point on the plain, at one of two observation platforms, the rising or setting sun appears between the towers on different days of the year. At the solstices the sun rises at the two opposite ends of the row, and on days in between it rises behind a tower or a gap in the middle. The gaps between towers mark the calendar to within a day or two.

That makes Chankillo a working calendar, one that let ancient people track the seasons for planting, harvests and ritual. The two observation points are on either side of the towers, and each lines up with a different part of the horizon. It is a clear, simple system that works without instruments, and it is more than two thousand years old. UNESCO listed the complex in 2021, recognising it as the oldest known solar observatory in the Americas, and the claim has been published in major scientific journals.

A visit rewards patience. Walk first to the observation points and look toward the ridge, then climb the hill to stand among the towers. Dawn and sunset are the best moments for photographs and for understanding the idea, but at midday the light is flat and the heat intense. Take water and a hat. A small visitor centre has information and a local guide can explain the details. Wind blows constantly and carries sand.

The road leads through the desert coast, mostly on the Pan-American Highway, with long straights and a stiff crosswind. Casma, the main town nearby, has fuel and food, and the seafood is fresh. The dry season, from April to December, is the best time. Summer is hot and bright.
t.cerro mucho malo@-9.5,-78.2:
Cerro Mucho Malo, the Hill of Much Evil, is the name locals give to the ridge on which Chankillo's thirteen towers stand, and the name probably refers to the difficulty of the terrain, bare, stony and exposed. It is a long, low spine of rock rising above the plain, and the towers run along its crest, a procession of squat stone structures with stairways and small chambers at the top. From the plain, the ridge looks small. From the top, it commands a wide view over the valley, with the green strip of the irrigated river on one side and the empty desert on the other.

The climb is short but hot, and the loose stone makes for tricky footing. In the dry air, even a short walk can be tiring, so take it steadily and carry water. The towers were built of stone and mud mortar, with carefully fitted blocks. Visitors can walk between them and see how they were placed. From their tops, sentries could have watched the plain for hours, though the main purpose was the sun, not the enemy.

Wind is a constant companion. It blows across the ridge with a steady force, whistling around the stones and lifting fine dust. In the early morning, the light is soft and golden, the air is still, and the temperatures are bearable. The best views are at dawn, and the sunset along the western coast is also fine, as the sun falls into the Pacific haze. The sky is usually clear, and at night the stars are brilliant.

Getting here involves a ride along the coastal Pan-American Highway, a mostly straight road across the desert. Casma is the nearest town of any size, with fuel and food, and there are other stations on the highway. Stops are widely spaced, so fill the tank when you can. On the road, expect fast trucks and buses, and give them room. The desert is dry for most of the year, and fog, known as garua, can blanket the coast in winter. Between April and December the weather is usually settled.
t.vladimir@56.1,40.4:
Vladimir was the capital of northeastern Russia in the twelfth century, long before Moscow mattered, and its main monuments are still the ones its princes built. It sits on a ridge above the Klyazma river, about two hundred kilometres east of Moscow, and today it is a city of over three hundred thousand with a quiet historic core and ordinary suburbs. Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky moved the centre of power here in the 1150s, and his successors poured their wealth into white limestone churches that are among the finest in the country.

The Assumption Cathedral, finished in 1160 and expanded later, stands on the edge of the ridge, its gold dome visible from far down the valley, and inside are frescoes by Andrei Rublev, the great icon painter, from the early fifteenth century. The Golden Gate, a defensive tower and gateway built in 1164, still stands in the middle of the town with a small church in its upper level. The nearby Cathedral of St Demetrius is covered in intricate carvings of animals, saints and plants in pale stone. Together with the churches of Suzdal and the little Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, these buildings form a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

The Intercession on the Nerl, at Bogolyubovo, a short ride from town, is a small white church standing by a meadow that floods in spring, so that it seems to float. It was built in 1165 and is often described as one of the most perfect small buildings in Russia. The walk across the fields to reach it is a pleasant one, particularly in early morning when mist hangs over the water.

For riders, the roads around Vladimir are gentle and unhurried, with long straight stretches between villages, farmland and birch woods. The M7 highway from Moscow is fast and busy with trucks, and the older roads give a better sense of the country, though surfaces can be rough, particularly after winter. Suzdal, to the north, and Murom, to the east, have a quiet charm, and the Oka river, one of the great rivers of central Russia, is worth seeing.

Vladimir has plenty of fuel, food and repairs, and the nearby towns of Kommunar and Bogolyubovo have a few services. Summer is warm and green, autumn golden, and winter cold and snowy, and honey, pickles and pies are good to try at local cafes.
t.rio abiseo national park@-7.7,-77.2:
There is no road to these coordinates, and that is the whole point of the place. Río Abiseo National Park covers a large block of the eastern Andes in the San Martín region of Peru, a tangle of steep cloud forest and high grassland where the mountains fall away toward the Amazon basin. It was set up in 1983 and is a World Heritage site for both its nature and its archaeology. Much of it has never been properly explored, and the interior is reachable only on foot after days of travel, with permits from the authorities.

The wildlife is exceptional because the terrain has protected it. The yellow-tailed woolly monkey, a species that was thought to be nearly extinct, lives here, and so do spectacled bears, mountain tapirs, jaguars and an extraordinary variety of birds and orchids. Mist hangs in the trees most mornings, the forest drips and smells of moss and wet leaf litter, and rivers run white through the gorges. In the park stand the ruins of Gran Pajatén and other stone settlements built into the hillsides, attributed to cultures older than the Incas, with round buildings decorated with carved slate patterns that look like birds and human figures.

For a motorcyclist, the practical choice is to ride the lower edges of the country. The roads of the region climb and drop through remarkably steep terrain, with narrow, winding strips of tarmac and gravel hugging the sides of valleys, and landslides in the rainy season from about November to April are frequent. Mud, fog, rockfalls and trucks on single-lane stretches demand patience, and a day's progress may be short. The dry months from May to September are far kinder, though the mountains still make their own weather.

There are no towns close to the coordinates, so plan fuel and food well in advance and carry spare supplies, a tyre repair kit and warm clothing, as the nights are cold at height. Larger towns on the approaches have stations and basic services, but they are far apart and quality varies. The park itself is a place to read about and respect rather than to visit casually, and anyone hoping to go in needs proper guidance and arrangements.
t.the prince castle in bogolyubovo@56.4,40:
A small correction before anything else: the castle in the label belongs to Bogolyubovo, a village near Vladimir, but the coordinates sit in the middle of Suzdal, about thirty-five kilometres north, so this text follows the coordinates. Prince Andrey Bogolyubsky built his fortified residence at Bogolyubovo in the 1150s and 1160s, after he moved the centre of power in northern Rus away from Kyiv, and a lone staircase tower from it still stands beside a later monastery. That prince also built the white stone cathedrals of Vladimir and the Golden Gate, which this ride is paired with, and the tiny church of the Intercession on the Nerl, which rises from a flood meadow like a white candle and is one of the most perfect small churches in Russia.

Suzdal itself is the heart of the old Golden Ring, a town of about eleven thousand people that was a princely seat in the Middle Ages, then a place of monasteries and merchants, and then, when the railway went elsewhere, simply forgotten. The result is a town that kept its low wooden houses, its many white churches and its monastery walls, so the skyline still looks seventeenth-century. The Kremlin stands on a bend of the Kamenka river, with the blue, star-spangled domes of the Nativity Cathedral, and the meadows along the river are dotted with wooden churches and windmills. Suzdal is also known for its honey mead, medovukha, and for pickled cucumbers, which have their own festival.

The country around is flat to gently rolling, a landscape of birch woods, wide fields and villages with carved wooden window frames. Roads are straight and quiet but can be badly patched, particularly after the freeze, and heavy trucks wear ruts into the surface, so the pace is steady. Summer is warm and green, and the autumn colours of birch and aspen are lovely, while winter closes the season with deep snow and ice. Mosquitoes by the river in the evening can be a nuisance.

Suzdal has fuel in the town, but Vladimir, about thirty-five kilometres to the south, has a wider choice of stations and services. Check the rules on documents and insurance for visitors before travelling, as regulations and sanctions affect foreign vehicles and travel in Russia. In town, a plate of pancakes and a glass of mead make a good break.
t.monastery of our savior and st euthymius:
At the northern edge of Suzdal, behind high brick walls with a dozen towers, stands the Monastery of Saint Euthymius, one of the most imposing fortified monasteries in Russia. It was founded in the fourteenth century by a monk from Nizhny Novgorod, and in the seventeenth century the walls were raised and the towers added when the Time of Troubles taught people to fear Polish raids. The whole complex looks more like a military fort than a place of prayer, and the cathedral inside, with its painted interior and ornate gilded iconostasis, shows how much wealth the monastery gathered through land and donations.

The grounds hold a bell tower where, at certain times of day, a bell-ringer performs a concert on the bells, and the sound rolling out over the town is memorable. Among those buried here is Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, who with Kuzma Minin raised the volunteer army that drove the Poles from Moscow in 1612, and whose statue stands in Red Square. In later centuries, the monastery served as a prison for people the state wanted out of the way, including religious dissidents and political prisoners, and part of the site still carries that grimness.

The setting is gentle, a grassy slope above the Kamenka river, with the town spread out to the south and a horizon of birch woods. From the walls you get the best view of the roofs, towers and domes of Suzdal, especially in the morning light. Summer weekends bring tour buses, and the best time is early, before the crowds. The ride in is easy, with quiet roads and slow traffic, and the cobbles and potholes of the old town call for care, particularly after rain.

For fuel and bigger services, you need to look to Vladimir, about thirty-five kilometres south, since Suzdal is a small town, though it will have basic stations. The nearby villages of Kideksha, with its early white-stone church of Saints Boris and Gleb, are a short ride to the east and can be combined with the visit. Rules on documents, insurance and permission for foreign visitors and vehicles in Russia change, so check them in good time before you leave, and travel with the correct paperwork. A glass of mead in a wooden tavern near the walls is the natural reward.
t.church of sts boris and gleb@56.4,40.5:
Kideksha is a village on a bend of the Nerl and Kamenka rivers, a short way from Suzdal, and if you could pick one place to see where the architecture of north-eastern Russia began, this would be it. The church of Saints Boris and Gleb, built in 1152 by Prince Yuri Dolgorukov, the founder of Moscow, is the oldest surviving white-stone building in the region. It is small, square and quiet, with a squat dome and thick walls, and the stone is a pale limestone that glows in the evening. The prince is said to have chosen the place because it lay at a meeting of rivers and trade routes, and an older fortified settlement stood on the mound beside it.

The two saints it honours were brothers, sons of Prince Vladimir, who in 1015 were killed by their older half-brother and became the first canonised saints of Rus. They accepted their deaths without a fight, and the tradition of such humble martyrdom ran deep in Russian religion. The church was damaged and rebuilt several times, and what you see is a mixture of the medieval core and later additions, with a seventeenth-century tent-roofed bell tower and a cluster of other buildings making up a small monastic group.

The village is a place of slow rural life, with wooden houses behind picket fences, geese on the green and a river meadow where cows graze. The approach from Suzdal takes only a few minutes on a country road through fields and birch woods, and the traffic is minimal outside the tourist season. The surface is fairly good, with a few frost heaves and potholes, and in spring the lower meadows can flood. In July the fields are full of flowers and the air smells of cut hay, and in the evening the light across the river is soft and gold.

Kideksha has more than eight thousand people on the figures available, though it feels much smaller, and has basic shops and a cafe. Fuel is more reliable in Suzdal or the larger city of Vladimir about forty kilometres to the south-west. The visit takes less than an hour but rewards a longer sit on the riverbank. Because rules on travel and vehicle documents for foreigners in Russia change, check the latest position before setting out.
t.kostroma@57.8,40.9:
Kostroma sits where the Kostroma river joins the Volga, and its position at the confluence made it a significant town for nearly nine centuries. The founding is attributed to Yuri Dolgoruky in the twelfth century, and from the Middle Ages it was a prosperous trading town, famous for its linen and flax. The Volga here is wide and slow, with long sandbars, and the waterfront is lined with a tidy promenade where people stroll in the evenings.

The great moment in Kostroma's history took place at the Ipatiev Monastery, a fortified complex with white walls and a tall bell tower on the river bank. In 1613 a delegation of nobles came here to ask the young Mikhail Romanov to accept the Russian crown, ending the Time of Troubles and starting the dynasty that ruled until 1917. The monastery is a vivid place, with a remarkable collection of old wooden buildings brought from the countryside gathered in an open-air museum nearby. The story of Ivan Susanin, a peasant who is said to have led a Polish force astray in the forest to protect the young tsar, is told in the town, and a statue of him stands in the main square.

Kostroma is also the home of the Snow Maiden. The playwright Alexander Ostrovsky set his fairy tale play there, and the town has adopted the character, with a small themed house for visitors. The older streets are lined with merchants' houses, and the central square has a fire tower from the early nineteenth century in the style of a neoclassical lookout, reminding you of the dangers of a wooden town.

The riding around Kostroma is mostly a matter of flat plains and slow river views. The road along the Volga to Plyos, a charming small town beloved by painters, is one of the best in the area, with views from the high bank over the river. Surfaces vary, and trucks, local buses and cattle are common on the smaller roads. In the summer there are plenty of mosquitoes near the water.

The city has everything for the traveller, including fuel, repair shops and good places to eat. Local dishes include fish from the Volga and the cheese that gave Kostroma a reputation across the country. Evening light on the water is lovely, and the best seasons are late spring and early autumn.
t.toliara@-23.4,43.7:
The RN7 ends at Toliara, a flat, sandy, sun-struck town on the south-west coast of Madagascar, where the highlands have been left far behind and the land is dry, thorny and bright. The town, sometimes still called Tulear, has about a hundred and fifteen thousand people, and it sits on the Mozambique Channel with wide streets, dusty pavements, handcarts and the pousse-pousse rickshaws that carry people everywhere. Nights are warm, days are hot and the sea breeze is a mercy.

The people of the coast are the Vezo, who live from the sea in dugout canoes with sails, and who are known for their skill at fishing and diving. Their villages, a few hours to the north at Ifaty and Mangily, are strung along a beach behind a coral reef, one of the longest in the Indian Ocean, and the outrigger sails against the setting sun are a sight to remember. Inland from the coast lies the spiny forest, a strange landscape of tall, thorny octopus trees, baobabs and euphorbias, adapted to the dry conditions, and found only in this part of the world. The Reniala reserve near Ifaty protects a good piece of it.

The road in is the long reward. After the Isalo massif, the RN7 descends in long, hot sweeps through dry savannah, and the last stretch to Toliara is flat and straight, with sand drifting over the surface and heavy trucks. There is a lot of heat, and distances between stations are long, so carry water and spare fuel. Sand tracks lead to the beaches, which can be difficult on a loaded motorbike. The best season is the dry winter, May to October, when the temperatures are bearable.

Toliara has fuel, banks, hotels and restaurants, and it is the sensible place to rest after the journey. Fresh seafood is cheap and good, with grilled lobster, fish and octopus, and a cold local beer on a terrace by the sea is a classic way to finish the trip. Bring cash, since cards are rarely accepted. Check the bike before heading farther, since parts are hard to find.
t.nizhny novgorod@56.3,44.0:
Nizhny Novgorod stands where the Oka flows into the Volga, a meeting of two enormous rivers that gives the city its character. The high bank on which the kremlin stands is a natural fortress, and the red-brick walls, built in the early sixteenth century, climb around the hill with thirteen towers still standing. From the ramparts you look out over the confluence and the cape called the Strelka, where the two streams run side by side for a while, one darker, one paler, before merging.

The city's history is long and varied. It was founded in 1221 as a frontier fortress against the Mordvins and Bulgars, and in 1612, during the Time of Troubles, a local butcher named Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky raised a volunteer army here that drove the Polish garrison out of Moscow. For centuries it hosted the great Nizhny Novgorod Fair, one of the biggest trading events in the empire. The writer Maxim Gorky was born here, and from 1932 to 1990 the whole city was called Gorky in his honor. During the Soviet period it was closed to foreigners because of its military factories, and it was where the physicist Andrei Sakharov lived in internal exile.

The streets reward walking. Bolshaya Pokrovskaya, the main pedestrian street, runs from the center to the Kremlin, and the Chkalov Stairs, a long flight of steps that descends toward the Volga, give a sweeping view. The city has about one and a quarter million people and a lively mix of old merchant houses, Soviet blocks and modern buildings. Traffic in the center can be heavy, and bridges over the Oka and the Volga become bottlenecks at rush hour.

For riders, the real treat lies outside. Heading up the Volga to Gorodets, with its painted wooden houses, and to Chkalovsk, birthplace of the pilot Valery Chkalov, you ride along a high bank with views over the water, on roads that range from smooth to rough. Summers are warm, autumn is golden and winter is long and cold. Fuel, food and repairs are available everywhere, and Bor, across the river, has more of the same.

Stop at the Strelka at dusk and watch the lights come on along both banks. It is one of the great river views of Russia.
